title: The first words, again
hookLine: salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah: once vocabulary, now a map; and a neighbor's peace
tomorrow: which story would you tell a kid who feels stuck?

cards: The first words anyone learns in a new language are tiny: hello, thanks, see you. This path started small too: bismillah was its very first word, and inshallah came a few days later.

Set them beside two more, salaam and alhamdulillah, and you have four little words. Back then they were vocabulary. Now, after the long road since, they look different: a map of a single day, and of a whole life.

teach.b: Salaam, peace: how you meet anyone, at any door. Bismillah: how you begin. The Qur'an opens with it, in Pickthall's words: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful."
Alhamdulillah: how you respond, the very next line: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Inshallah: how you face tomorrow.
The Qur'an tells the Prophet never to say of anything, I'll do that tomorrow, without adding: if Allah wills. Meet, begin, thank, hope. That's a day.
Stretch it out, and it's a life. Now a neighbor. Jewish neighbors greet with peace too, shalom aleichem, peace be upon you.
And the Torah's blessing for the people ends on it, in the JPS words: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."
What's shared: both put peace into the most ordinary moment there is, hello.
One honest difference: in the Torah, that blessing is given to Aaron and his sons, the priests, to say over the people.
As-salamu alaykum is said by anyone to anyone, and the Qur'an asks the one greeted to answer with the same or better.
And a line for anyone who greets you: in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says spreading salaam is how people come to love one another.

how: Muslims greet with as-salamu alaykum and answer wa alaykum as-salam, say bismillah before eating, starting work or travel, alhamdulillah after meals and good news, and inshallah when speaking of the future.

o: the first verses of the Qur'an a child memorizes
salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah: a map of life
the words said on becoming Muslim, in order

games.q: the four words — tap the pairs.
p: how you begin: in Allah's name
how you respond: praise to Allah
how you face tomorrow: if Allah wills

s: inshallah is just a polite way of saying no
the Qur'an asks believers to add 'if Allah wills' to any plan for tomorrow; it's hope, handed over.
the Qur'an's opening line is 'In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful'
bismillah opens al-Fatiha, in Pickthall's words.
salaam and the Torah's priestly blessing work the same way
both give peace; the Torah's blessing is given to the priests to say over the people, while salaam is said by anyone to anyone.

games.q: a new coworker, who is Jewish, greets you warmly with 'shalom aleichem.' what reply honors both of you?
o: return the peace: 'and peace to you,' or 'wa alaykum as-salam.'
smile, then gently explain that Muslims say salaam instead.
keep it neutral and skip religious greetings at work.
games.why: the Qur'an asks the one greeted to answer with the same or better. peace offered, peace returned.

practice: Say the four slowly, one on each breath: salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah. With each one, name the moment in your own day where it belongs: a door, a start, a thank-you, a plan. Go around again if there's time.

wordCard.voice: The first words: salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah. Meet in peace, begin with Allah's name, thank Him, and leave tomorrow in His hands.

orig.note: Arabic: in the name of Allah; the first words of the Qur'an.

carryVoice: Keep this one for the summit: four words, a whole life, from the first door to the last. Day one of the summit, counted.
